newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Georgia wants action against separatists.
newsitem.headline: Georgia wants action against separatists.

text.p: Facing rebellions since the breakup of the Soviet Union, Georgia's foreign minister on Monday said "aggressive separatism" should be punished by sanctions and other measures.

"On this question, the world community has no right to take the position of an outside observer, because countries and entire regions are subjected to separatism," Irakliy Menagarishvili told the General Assembly.

Some 250,000 Georgians fled the Abkhazia region in 1993 when separatists, backed by mercenaries and arms from Russia's northern Caucasus region, drove out Georgian government troops in a lightning campaign. Negotiations by Russia and the United Nations to resolve the conflict have remained deadlocked.

Menagarishvili said sanctions, particularly an arms embargo, should be imposed on violent separatist movements and economic assistance given to those who have to deal with them. If this doesn't work, then the culprits should stand before an international tribunal, he said.
"Aggressive separatism is not a new phenomenon, but it has only comparatively recently come into the focus of the world community," he said.

He said no matter what the underlying reasons for separatist movements, they had one thing in common: "Under the banner of self-determination of suppressed people, regimes are created on the ideological basis of terrorism," he said.

Under international law, self-determination was frequently provided to former colonies and other states. But he said it was unacceptable when such a principle was misused by national minorities that utilized ethnic cleansing "as the main tool of vengeance against other nations and ethnic groups."

He said ethnic cleansing, accompanied by mass killing, continued even today in Abkhazia, whose leaders have raised the expulsion of the Georgia population to the level of state policy. Proposals for wide-reaching automony for the region have fallen on deaf ears.

"The response of the world community, in relation to separatism, as a rule is nearly always late and consequently inadequate to existing conditions. Simply speaking we suffer from inertia, or if you wish, from a delayed reaction," he said.
The Security Council began deliberations on the issue in July 1993 but took three years to "call an aggressor an aggressor and a criminal a criminal and a victim a victim," the foreign minister said.
